description: How wages are set by the demand for and supply of labour, and why different jobs pay very differently.
content_html:
What Is the Labour Market?

The labour market is like any other market — it brings together buyers and sellers to agree on a price. The “price” in this market is the wage, and the goods being traded are workers’ time and skills. Firms are the buyers of labour; workers are the sellers. When a supermarket recruits checkout staff, or a hospital hires nurses, or a tech company takes on developers, they are all operating in the labour market.

Just as with goods and services, the wage rate in a labour market is determined by the interaction of demand and supply. Understanding this helps explain why a surgeon earns far more than a shelf-stacker, and why footballers earn more than firefighters.

The Demand for Labour

The demand for labour comes from firms. Crucially, firms do not hire workers for the sake of it — they hire workers because those workers help produce goods or services that customers will buy. This makes the demand for labour a derived demand. The demand for nurses is derived from the demand for healthcare; the demand for builders is derived from the demand for new homes.

When the wage rate rises, employing workers becomes more expensive. Firms respond by cutting the number of workers they hire, perhaps using machinery instead, or reducing output. Conversely, when wages fall, firms are willing to take on more workers. This gives the labour demand curve its characteristic downward slope: at higher wage rates, less labour is demanded.

Several factors can shift the demand for labour:

  • The demand for the final product — if demand for electric vehicles rises sharply, car manufacturers need more production workers. The demand for labour shifts outward.
  • Labour productivity — if workers become more productive (they produce more per hour), they become more valuable to the firm, so demand for them rises at every wage rate.
  • Technology — automation and artificial intelligence can substitute for workers in some roles, shifting demand for that type of labour inward. At the same time, new technologies create demand for workers who can operate and maintain new systems.
Key Fact

The demand for labour is derived demand — firms hire workers only because consumers demand the goods or services those workers produce. A fall in consumer demand for a product will therefore reduce the demand for the workers who make it.

The Supply of Labour

The supply of labour comes from workers who are willing and able to work at a given wage rate. The labour supply curve slopes upward: as wages rise, more people are attracted into that occupation. A higher hourly rate for warehouse work might draw in students, part-time workers and career-changers who would not previously have applied.

Several factors shift the supply of labour:

  • The size of the working population — immigration, changes in the retirement age, or more women entering the workforce all increase the overall supply of labour.
  • Skills and qualifications — jobs requiring rare skills (such as a neurosurgeon or a specialist engineer) have very low supply because few people have the necessary training.
  • Non-wage factors — some jobs attract workers even at lower wages because they offer other benefits: social status, interesting work, flexible hours, or job security. Teaching and social work often fall into this category.
  • Trade union membership — trade unions can restrict entry to certain occupations, effectively reducing the supply of labour and keeping wages higher.

A movement along the supply curve happens when the wage rate itself changes. If an employer raises pay from £11 to £13 per hour, more workers are willing to take the job — this is a movement up along the existing supply curve, not a shift.

A shift of the supply curve happens when something other than the wage changes. For example, if the government raises the school leaving age, fewer young workers are available — the supply curve shifts to the left. Or if a new university course suddenly produces thousands of qualified nurses, the supply curve shifts to the right, pushing the equilibrium wage down.

How Wages Are Determined

The equilibrium wage in a labour market is set where the demand for labour equals the supply of labour. Imagine the market for software developers. Demand is high because technology firms compete fiercely for coding talent. Supply is limited because coding requires specific skills and several years of training. This combination of high demand and low supply pushes the equilibrium wage upward — and explains why software developers tend to be well paid.

By contrast, think about the market for general retail assistants. The skills required are relatively low, so the supply is large (many people can do the job). Meanwhile, the growth of online shopping has reduced demand for in-store staff. High supply and lower demand mean the equilibrium wage stays close to the minimum wage.

Key Fact

The equilibrium wage is where labour demand meets labour supply. A rise in demand for labour (or a fall in supply) pushes wages up. A fall in demand (or rise in supply) pushes wages down. The wage signals to workers whether to enter or leave a particular occupation.

Wage Differentials

Wage differentials are the gaps in pay between different jobs. These differentials exist for several reasons:

  • Skill and qualifications — jobs requiring years of training (medicine, law, engineering) restrict supply, pushing wages higher. A consultant surgeon earns more than a care worker because far fewer people can do the job.
  • Responsibility and decision-making — managers and executives bear significant consequences if they make poor decisions. Higher pay compensates for this responsibility.
  • Danger and unpleasant conditions — jobs that carry physical risk (offshore oil workers, demolition workers) or that are simply unpleasant may need a compensating pay premium to attract workers.
  • Experience — more experienced workers typically earn more because their accumulated knowledge makes them more productive.
  • Gender and discrimination — historically, labour markets have not always reflected pure supply and demand. Discrimination based on gender, ethnicity or background can result in workers being paid less than their productivity would suggest. Governments have introduced legislation to combat this.

A trade union is an organisation that represents workers and negotiates with employers. By acting collectively, unions give workers more bargaining power than they would have individually. A single worker threatening to quit is easy to replace; a union threatening a strike is not.

Trade unions can push wages above the free-market equilibrium. They do this by collective bargaining — negotiating on behalf of all their members at once. If they succeed in raising wages, the quantity of labour demanded may fall (as firms respond to higher costs), potentially leading to some job losses. The trade-off between higher wages for those in work and fewer jobs overall is one of the central debates about trade union power.

The National Minimum Wage and the National Living Wage

The government sets legal wage floors to protect low-paid workers. The National Minimum Wage applies to workers aged 16 and over, with different rates for different age groups. The National Living Wage is a higher rate applied to workers aged 21 and over.

Setting a wage floor above the free-market equilibrium has two effects. On the positive side, workers who keep their jobs receive higher pay, which can reduce poverty and boost consumer spending. On the negative side, if the minimum wage is set significantly above equilibrium, some firms may reduce their workforce, cut hours, or delay hiring — creating unemployment.

Whether the minimum wage causes unemployment depends heavily on the circumstances. In a labour market where firms have significant power over wages (for example, a single large employer in a small town), a minimum wage can actually increase both wages and employment simultaneously. In a highly competitive labour market, the effect on employment is more likely to be negative.

Gross Pay and Net Pay

When employers and employees agree on a wage, the figure they discuss is usually gross pay — the full amount before any deductions. What a worker actually receives in their bank account is net pay, also called take-home pay. The difference between the two consists mainly of income tax (a direct tax paid to HMRC) and National Insurance Contributions.

For example, using 2025-26 rates (personal allowance £12,570, income tax 20%, employee National Insurance 8%), a worker earning £30,000 per year in gross pay would pay income tax of £3,486 and National Insurance of £1,394, leaving net pay of roughly £25,100. Calculating gross and net pay is a key quantitative skill in GCSE Economics.
exam_tip_html: Labour market questions reward explicit chains of reasoning. When asked to “Explain” something, always link cause to effect: “Supply of skilled workers is low → firms must offer higher wages to attract them → equilibrium wage rises.” For a “Calculate” question on gross or net pay, show your working clearly — write the formula, substitute the numbers, and state the answer with a £ sign and “per year” or “per hour”. For Evaluate questions, resist simply listing reasons why wages differ — instead, weigh them: the most important factor is usually the skill and qualification barrier, because it most directly restricts supply. Support your judgement by saying “it depends on” whether the job market is competitive or dominated by a small number of employers.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Wages are set by the demand and supply of labour. Demand is derived from consumer demand for goods and services; supply depends on the number of qualified workers available. Where demand is high and supply is low, wages are pushed up.
  • Wage differentials reflect differences in skill, qualifications, danger, responsibility and market power. Trade unions can raise wages above the free-market equilibrium through collective bargaining.
  • The National Minimum Wage sets a legal pay floor to protect low-paid workers; gross pay is the total earned before tax, while net (take-home) pay is what remains after income tax and National Insurance are deducted.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes derived demand for labour?
A) The demand created when workers offer their services to more than one employer
B) The demand for workers that arises because of consumer demand for the goods or services they produce
C) The demand for labour that falls as wages rise
D) The demand for workers in overseas labour markets
practice_questions.marks: B) The demand for workers that arises because of consumer demand for the goods or services they produce [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A worker earns a gross annual salary of £28,000. Using the 2025-26 rates (personal allowance £12,570; income tax rate 20% on earnings above the personal allowance; employee National Insurance rate 8% on earnings above the personal allowance), calculate the worker's net annual pay. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for the correct method: Income tax = (£28,000 − £12,570) × 20% = £15,430 × 0.20 = £3,086; National Insurance = (£28,000 − £12,570) × 8% = £15,430 × 0.08 = £1,234.40; Net pay = £28,000 − £3,086 − £1,234.40.
1 mark for the correct answer of £23,679.60 per year.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why a brain surgeon earns a higher wage than a supermarket cashier.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for identifying a relevant reason, e.g. the supply of brain surgeons is very low because the job requires many years of specialist training and qualifications.
1 mark for developing this: because so few people have the necessary skills, firms (hospitals) must offer a much higher wage to attract workers.
1 mark for linking to the labour market outcome: this low supply relative to high demand pushes the equilibrium wage up significantly compared to a job requiring few qualifications.

practice_questions.text: A government introduces a National Minimum Wage set above the current market equilibrium for workers in the hospitality industry. Using demand and supply analysis of the labour market, explain how this might affect workers and employers in the hospitality industry.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for stating the effect on wages: workers who remain employed receive higher pay than before.
1 mark for developing the benefit: higher wages increase workers' disposable income and reduce poverty among low-paid hospitality staff.
1 mark for stating the effect on employers: firms face higher wage costs, so the quantity of labour demanded falls as the minimum wage is above equilibrium.
1 mark for developing the drawback: some hospitality businesses may reduce staff hours, automate tasks (e.g. self-service kiosks) or hire fewer new workers, leading to unemployment for some low-paid workers.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a significant rise in the popularity of electric vehicles might affect wages in the UK car manufacturing industry.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A sustained chain of reasoning connecting rising consumer demand for electric vehicles → increased derived demand for workers in EV manufacturing → demand curve for EV workers shifts right → upward pressure on wages → higher equilibrium wage. Candidate extends the chain: firms invest in training and retooling → productivity may rise → demand rises further. May identify that traditional combustion-engine workers face falling demand → their wages are under downward pressure → wage differentials within the industry widen. Logical conclusion reached.
Secure (3–4 marks): Clear demand-and-supply chain applied to the labour market. At least two steps of reasoning. May be one-sided (only rising demand for EV workers, without analysing falling demand for combustion workers).
Developing (2 marks): Some correct reasoning (e.g. demand for labour rises, wages go up) but limited development or chain incomplete.
Emerging (1 mark): Simple point that wages might rise or that more workers are needed, without development.

practice_questions.text: 'Trade unions always benefit workers.' Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
Trade unions negotiate collectively, giving workers far more bargaining power than individuals acting alone. A union threatening industrial action can secure wage rises above the free-market equilibrium. Unions also protect workers from unfair dismissal, unsafe conditions and excessive hours — benefits that go beyond pay. In industries where a single employer dominates (such as a large factory in a small town), unions counterbalance that employer's power and prevent exploitation.

Arguments against:
If trade unions successfully push wages above the equilibrium, firms respond by demanding less labour, potentially causing unemployment among the very workers unions aim to protect. Unions tend to benefit their existing members rather than workers outside the sector. Strikes can harm consumers and damage the firm's competitiveness. Rigid union agreements can also reduce flexibility, making it harder for firms to adapt to changing market conditions, which may accelerate automation.

Judgement:
The extent to which trade unions benefit workers depends on the structure of the labour market. In a market where employers have significant power over wages, unions genuinely raise pay and improve conditions without causing significant unemployment. In a highly competitive labour market, pushing wages above equilibrium is more likely to reduce employment. It also depends on the time period: in the short run unions may raise wages; in the long run firms may invest in automation to reduce their reliance on unionised labour.

Mastering (8–9 marks): Balanced analysis of both sides with a specific, supported judgement that uses at least one ‘it depends on’ condition (e.g. degree of employer market power, competitiveness of the labour market). Chains of reasoning run to their conclusion.
Secure (6–7 marks): Both sides developed with some supporting reasoning; judgement present but may be partially generic.
Developing (3–5 marks): Some relevant analysis; may be one-sided or judgement absent/unsupported.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Simple points for or against with little development.

knowledge_checks.q: What is meant by 'derived demand' for labour?
options: Workers demand higher wages over time as living costs rise
The demand for workers rises because more firms enter the market
The demand for labour comes from consumer demand for the goods or services workers produce
Employers demand labour derived from their profit targets

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is most likely to increase the supply of labour in a particular occupation?
options: A rise in the wage rate for that job
A fall in the number of people qualified to do the job
An increase in training programmes producing more qualified workers
Stronger trade union restrictions on entry to the profession

knowledge_checks.q: The wage rate is determined by the _____ for labour and the supply of labour.
_____ pay is the total amount a worker earns before deductions such as income tax are removed.
Match each term to its correct meaning:
right: Demand for workers that exists because of demand for what they produce
A difference in pay between different jobs or workers
An organisation that negotiates pay and conditions on behalf of workers

flashcard_questions.q: What is meant by the term 'wage'?
flashcard_questions.a: The payment workers receive in exchange for their labour.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is the demand for labour described as derived demand?
flashcard_questions.a: Firms hire workers only because consumers demand the goods or services those workers produce.

flashcard_questions.q: What shape does the labour demand curve have, and why?
flashcard_questions.a: Downward sloping — at higher wages, firms hire fewer workers as labour becomes more expensive.

flashcard_questions.q: What shape does the labour supply curve have, and why?
flashcard_questions.a: Upward sloping — higher wages attract more workers into that occupation.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one factor that shifts the demand for labour to the right.
flashcard_questions.a: A rise in consumer demand for the final good or service produced by those workers.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one factor that would shift the supply of labour to the left.
flashcard_questions.a: A fall in the number of qualified workers, e.g. fewer people completing required training.
A difference in pay between different jobs, workers, industries or regions.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one reason why surgeons earn more than shop assistants.
flashcard_questions.a: Surgery requires rare specialist qualifications, restricting supply and pushing the equilibrium wage up.
An organisation that represents workers and negotiates pay and conditions with employers.

flashcard_questions.q: How can a trade union push wages above the free-market equilibrium?
flashcard_questions.a: By collective bargaining — negotiating on behalf of all members, backed by the threat of strike action.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the National Minimum Wage?
flashcard_questions.a: The lowest hourly rate employers are legally allowed to pay workers, set by the government.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the net pay for a worker whose gross pay is £25,000 and total deductions are £4,200?
What is the difference between gross pay and net pay?
flashcard_questions.a: Gross pay is total earnings before deductions; net pay is what remains after tax and National Insurance.

glossary_terms.definition: The payment workers receive in exchange for their labour, typically expressed as an hourly rate, weekly wage, or annual salary.
Demand for a factor of production (such as labour) that arises because of the demand for the goods or services it produces.
Differences in pay between individuals, occupations, industries or regions.
An organisation of workers that negotiates with employers on pay, working conditions and job security on behalf of its members.
The lowest hourly rate that employers are legally allowed to pay workers, set by the government.
The total amount earned before any deductions such as income tax and National Insurance.
The amount a worker takes home after deductions such as income tax and National Insurance Contributions have been removed.
